    #136541. Why brands are writing no-AI clauses into creator deals

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (688 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    Why brands are writing no-AI clauses into creator deals

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (688 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, join us Dec.
    • Influencer marketing contracts have become a focal point in the creator economy.
    • “We actually are seeing more and more contracts including language around the creator not being able to use AI in their content for these campaigns,” stated Kurt Stadelman, vp of talent at creator marketing firm Pearpop, in a conversation with Digiday managing editor Sara Jerde during Digiday’s recent Creator Strategies event.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Influencer marketing contracts have become a focal point in the creator economy. There’s heightened attention being paid by brands, creators and creators’ representatives to deal terms, such as usage rights, exclusivity and payment terms. But among the newest addendums is AI usage.

    “We actually are seeing more and more contracts including language around the creator not being able to use AI in their content for these campaigns,” stated Kurt Stadelman, vp of talent at creator marketing firm Pearpop, in a conversation with Digiday managing editor Sara Jerde during Digiday’s recent Creator Strategies event.

    Creators are actually welcoming brands’ no-AI demands, he mentioned. Creators are already concerned about generative AI being used to create content and crowd out creators from people’s feeds. So brands forbidding AI-generated content from creators signals a commitment by brands to human-made content, said Stadelman.

    Sources indicate that but what counts as AI-generated content? Does it prohibit the creator from using AI tools in any part of their process?

    In a recent development, “We’ve had to specify that a few times just to make sure, because obviously you want the creator to be able to use AI tools in the background when they’re developing their concept or their script. Even utilizing AI to analyze their past performance of their content and advise them on their strategy moving forward. And I think brands should probably embrace that because it ultimately helps the creator deliver the best version of themselves and the best content possible,” said Stadelman.

    Here are a few highlights from the conversation, which have been edited for length and clarity.

    It’s way too risky to be only utilizing organic posting for creator campaigns and just hoping that the right people see it. We are seeing more and more brands utilize paid behind whether it’s white-listing or utilizing the creator content as an ad unit for themselves on their own channels. Along with that comes, obviously, you have to write the paid usage rights into the contract, and most brands are good about that.

    The wrong length for usage rights.

    Recent findings suggest that usage in perpetuity should never be agreed to. That’s a dangerous place to be for a creator and can negatively impact their future collaborations with other brands in the same category. Exclusivity, obviously, is quite difficult for a lot of creators if they agree to a longer exclusivity term than they should. That limits their options moving forward.

    The right length for usage rights.

    Recent findings suggest that sometimes you’ll see proposed terms that are just a little too lengthy with the usage rights. We push back on that sometimes. I don’t think there’s any reason to be agreeing upfront to any more than six months of paid usage. Even that’s a bit lengthy. Starting it at three months if they’re really wanting to utilize paid with the campaign, that makes sense. Even up to six months is fine in most cases. But once you get to that point six months from now, you can reassess and extend if you’d like. But I don’t think there’s any reason to go beyond that in the initial contract.

    In a recent development, we always push for shorter payment terms. If somebody’s asking for net-90, we try to push for net-60 or, ideally, net-30. But I understand that some brands have their standard operating procedures there, which is fine. But we just ask that they honor those payment terms, which is a whole other issue that we’re seeing happen more and more, is that brands are just not honoring these payment terms that they’ve themselves written into the contract.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    Banking gets a helping hand in media modeling from SpendSight

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (774 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • It’s easy to know what your bank balance is, in the age of apps and online banking.
    • Mediastruction, an independent media agency that two years ago debuted FutureSight, a SaaS platform dedicated to speeding up media mix modeling, is drilling into specific industries.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    It’s easy to know what your bank balance is, in the age of apps and online banking. It’s not as easy for banks to know how effective their marketing efforts are.

    Mediastruction, an independent media agency that two years ago debuted FutureSight, a SaaS platform dedicated to speeding up media mix modeling, is drilling into specific industries.

    Sources indicate that the brainchild of Marilois Snowman, who founded Mediastruction and FutureSight, SpendSight puts a specific lens onto the banking industry. It’s a free benchmarking tool that enables bank marketers to evaluate their media budgets to see if their spending aligns with their peers.

    Snowman noted conversations with clients and with other banks that aren’t yet clients told her there’s an information gap in the sector. “It’s a problem for mid market in general,” she explained in reference to other subscription media tools. “Sometimes mid-market brands don’t show up at all, or then they’re just wildly inaccurate.”.

    Industry observers note that for small banks, this information is pretty vital, agreed Mark Gibson, marketing practice leader at Capital Performance Group. “It’s not uncommon in the banking industry to have one or two people in the marketing department, and maybe not even an ad or media agency,” he noted. “Media is like you know 1/20th of your job, so by definition, you’re not going to be very sophisticated about about what media is available and how you should allocate it. For that kind of advertiser, this kind of stuff can be really valuable.”.

    Snowman also noted that some media, from search to social and CTV, aren’t even properly tracked by other services. “Given the percentage of investment that is digital media these days — I mean, what isn’t digital media? — it just seems to be a big gap.”.

    Mediastruction built SpendSight from a proprietary 2026 survey of financial institution marketers, and Snowman noted it’s the first of its kind to capture how banks and credit unions actually split paid media dollars across channels. To date, about 100 different banks and credit unions have participated in the survey, giving them access to the findings.

    Any bank marketer enters their budget and channel mix, which lets SpendSight generate a side-by-side comparison against the peer average, flagging where they’re over- or under-invested. All inputs and responses to the survey remain anonymous and the underlying survey data is never exposed.

    “All of that kind of discussion is really helpful for marketing teams to bring to executive leadership, and then to be able to sell through shifts in media looks and modeling engagements,” said Snowman.

    So what has SpendSight determined? Initial results show some patterns with how banks and financial services have been marketing, and which media channels they’re relying on. Although it comes as no surprise that digital performance channels make up about 51% of the average media mix, broadcast and traditional media (linear TV, radio, print, out-of-home) still account for roughly 38%. (Interestingly, the American Bankers Association’s Banking Journal cited more than 60% digital spend, which Snowman attributed to differing channel definitions.).

    Within digital, paid search and paid social represent more than one-fourth of average spend (13.7% and 13.0%, respectively). Paid search is the most widely used channel, with 96% of institutions investing in it. As for other media, direct mail makes up 7.4% of the average mix and is used by 82% of institutions, which is more than linear TV, display, and online video (as anyone knows who gets mail at home).

    In a recent development, gibson at Capital Performance Group, which participates in multiple surveys for banking including SpendSight, noted the reason he thinks SpendSight goes one step farther. “While [other studies] provide some useful benchmarking in terms of how much banks spend overall, and what various media are used, they don’t quantify the spend by media mix or by media channel,” he said. “That’s the new innovation that this tool does.”.

    According to recent reports, it also gives Mediastruction lead generation to build up its potential client base with financial firms, which Snowman acknowledged. “What we really want to sell through is FutureSight’s modeling. We can use this as a free tool to get to know us to offer something of benefit to potential clients, that’s what our goal is.”.

    #136535. Breaking: In Graphic Detail: How shoppers are adopting AI for product research ahead of Black Friday

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (700 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: In Graphic Detail: How shoppers are adopting AI for product research ahead of Black Friday

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (700 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.
    • Sources indicate that marketers are shifting ad dollars toward performance channels as the vital Black Friday/Cyber Monday trading period approaches.
    • Recent findings suggest that the places they find information about brands, the sources that information is based on, and what they do with that information are all changing.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Sources indicate that marketers are shifting ad dollars toward performance channels as the vital Black Friday/Cyber Monday trading period approaches. Yet the way consumers use search — a crucial channel within performance marketing — is evolving rapidly, as they adopt generative AI tools like Gemini and ChatGPT to aid their purchasing decisions.

    Recent findings suggest that the places they find information about brands, the sources that information is based on, and what they do with that information are all changing. Meanwhile, audience adoption of AI research is far from uniform across generations and markets, further complicating the picture.

    “Black Friday used to be won in the final week with the deepest discount and the loudest media,” noted Jonathan Verrall, vp of SEO at Jellyfish. “Now AI writes the shortlist weeks earlier from the sources shoppers trust. Advertisers who treat Black Friday as pure promo media are already late. The winners will plan earned, owned and paid together from October and give AI data it can believe.”.

    What is certain is that the way brands seek to influence consumers during product discovery and research is shifting. With the year’s biggest sales event around the corner, read on for a data snapshot of the state of product discovery.

    Industry observers note that according to a survey of 2,800 shoppers in the U.S. and U.K. conducted by Brainlabs in 2025 and 2026, the percentage of consumers using AI for product research rose on average from 6% last year to 13%. Clearly, more shoppers are using AI tools to compare and research the products they’re considering. While search engines themselves still led consumer practices, sources like Amazon and YouTube slipped.

    Industry observers note that A Jellyfish study of citation sources, using U.K. Black Friday-related prompts the week beginning Nov. 16, found third-party sources leading the pack. That means blogs, news articles and comparison sites counted for more than brands’ own websites or retail listings in influencing AI chatbot representations of a brand or a product.

    Sources indicate that this is borne out by other studies. In an analysis run for an unnamed client, PMG found a brand’s website supplied just 24 out of 203 links cited in AI answers recommending the client’s products. Only 22 went directly to its homepage.

    Even if they only account for a minority of citations, brands’ own sites, platforms and retailer listings are areas that an advertiser can control. Zooming in, not all retail platforms are equal, either. Amazon, Costco and Etsy’s sites have lost share of citations in recent quarters, while Target and Walmart have gained in recent months, according to data from Tinuiti and Profound.

    The hope that they might influence shoppers using AI tools for product discovery has been one of the motivations driving marketing dollars toward ChatGPT. Ad spend has risen month-on-month, according to estimates by AdClarity, which estimated total spend on the platform to have reached $116.6 million in October, with U.S. brands accounting for 64%. (The above chart is in millions of dollars.).

    Issues with measurability and evidence that ChatGPT ads lead to greater conversions, however, may hold brands back from accelerating that spend as much as OpenAI execs would like.

    According to recent reports, according to Bain, two-thirds of consumers use AI tools for general research, while 42% specifically use them to research products. But there are variations across generations.

    The McKinsey Agentic Commerce Consumer Survey, June 2026, surveyed 5,800 shoppers who’s used AI chatbots or search tools for a shopping task in the last three months. It found middle-aged and younger consumers are embracing the tech while older shoppers (who still hold plenty of disposable income) aren’t. It’s an crucial distinction for brands targeting consumers in specific stages of their lives.

    As social trends accelerate, brands like General Mills are scoring creator posts for shareability to bridge the gap between organic buzz and paid media.

    Dick’s is betting that youth sports can fuel its next phase of ad growth through GameChanger—if it can overcome limits on scale.

    As Black Friday Cyber Monday rapidly approaches, brands are most focused on acquiring new customers this holiday season.

    #136531. The clipping economy is changing as platforms crack down and creators seek control

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1302 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Digiday ↗ Open Full Page

    The clipping economy is changing as platforms crack down and creators seek control

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1302 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that join us Dec.
    • Depending on who you ask in the creator economy, they might say that clipping is dead.
    • Sources indicate that the practice of sharing short clips from long-form content to boost the original content’s audience or promote a brand, exploded in popularity over the last few years, with major creators like Jimmy “MrBeast” Donaldson, Cody “Clix” Conrod, and Eric “Airrack” Decker starting their own clipping companies.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Depending on who you ask in the creator economy, they might say that clipping is dead.

    Sources indicate that the practice of sharing short clips from long-form content to boost the original content’s audience or promote a brand, exploded in popularity over the last few years, with major creators like Jimmy “MrBeast” Donaldson, Cody “Clix” Conrod, and Eric “Airrack” Decker starting their own clipping companies. It catapulted certain creators into the spotlight and encouraged brands to hire clippers to give their branded partnerships extra airtime.

    In short, what began as fans sharing clips has grown into a billion-dollar distribution business.

    But some platforms are now tightening the rules around clipping. TikTok and YouTube have been cracking down on non-original and mass reposting content. Last week, Instagram added a content protection feature previously available only on Facebook, which lets eligible creators automatically identify videos matching their original content. They can now see how those videos perform and decide whether to hide them from people on the platform, add a credit link, or let the videos stay up. That gives creators more visibility and control over where their content appears, making clipping less of an open-ended reporting play and more subject to the original creator’s say.

    “Creators deserve credit for the work they make,” a Meta spokesperson told Digiday. “[This] builds on our broader efforts to prioritize and reward original content and creativity over re-uploaded posts that don’t add a unique perspective or meaningful edits.”.

    And yet, platforms aren’t all moving in the same direction: Twitch is investing further into clipping to try and claw back the short-form real estate it’s ceded to other platforms. To understand what’s driving these diverging approaches, and what they mean in practice, Digiday spoke with seven experts across the clipping ecosystem.

    “Ask 10 people [what clipping is] and you’ll probably get eight different answers,” noted Darren Clover, CEO of creator-led holding company Full Box Inc., which owns Reach Clipping. “We define clipping as skilled editors taking existing source material and transforming it into unique pieces of short-form content…Those videos are then distributed across individual social accounts. That’s very different from downloading someone else’s TikTok and reposting the exact same video across hundreds of accounts.”.

    Industry observers note that opinions also differ around whether clipping works as a performance marketing channel or if it’s just a good distribution method. A few days ago, Brian Blum, host of the Only Sweat Equity podcast, posted on X that clipping “has actually always been dead.” He told Digiday he meant that it has never worked as a performance marketing channel.

    Sources indicate that blum’s concern is that clipping can produce impressive view counts without reaching people likely to buy. He said campaigns can be vulnerable to fraud and attract audiences that may not be a fit for the product.

    “It doesn’t have necessary protections to prevent viewbotting or fraud…So you’re actually just lighting money on fire,” he remarked.

    Nikolai Amirzadeh, co-founded of clipping company Clip Tech, said clips can function as both marketing and distribution tools if the clipping company in question does the work to ensure views are valid.

    “It is priced like performance, you pay per 1,000 verified views and nothing for clips that flop. It behaves like earned media, because it is native posts from real accounts, not ads. Brands typically pay $1 to $4 per thousand verified views, against $10 to $80 or more for traditional paid social,” Amirzadeh said. “Anything that looks off goes to the fraud team, and the clipper is not paid until it is cleared. A view is still a view by each platform’s own definition, which is a low bar. That is why the serious brands look at the top clips, watch time and what happens downstream, not just the view total.”.

    Then there’s the question of control: As clipping spreads and platforms tighten their rules, creators and their partners are increasingly concerned about how clips are edited and shared, and whether they could create brand-safety risks.

    Industry observers note that “Clipping is kind of a double-edged sword. It can help creators gain visibility and show that people value their content, but it could also get them flagged as spam,” remarked Ashray Urs, head of Streamlabs.

    It has been revealed that that lack of control gives creators and their managers pause, according to Reed Duchscher, CEO of Night Management. “It’s hard to control any of it,” he said. “Even when you put out a bounty for someone to clip something, you still have very limited control of what is posted, how it’s posted,” he added, pointing to the common practice of people clipping streamers out of context to farm outrage or drama.

    Instead, their clients, like mega creator Kai Cenat, have their own in-house clippers, which allows for more control and, crucially, legitimate measurement.

    Recent findings suggest that expect this to be an increasingly popular approach in the next year. “Sometimes with these clipping companies you can’t understand if the views are legitimate or not…you don’t know if they’re paid views or not paid views because you’re not controlling the TikTok accounts and not posting the videos. So we’re a little nervous about that,” Duchscher said.

    With platforms cracking down on recycled content, the age of the clip farm may be over. But clipping itself isn’t.

    Mustafa Aijaz, vp of media company SoaR, thinks clipping is no longer a low-effort gold rush. “A quick cut and post won’t get you very far,” he said. “You need a different caption, some commentary, or a breakdown — something that adds to the raw clip itself. If you’re different, the platform treats you differently. But if you look exactly like the other posts, you’ll likely be throttled.”.

    According to recent reports, and as the demand for clips has grown, some have leaned into the more negative aspects of clipping, like taking creators out of context or clipping moments that are less than flattering. This influx of negative framing or drama farming has shifted creators’ opinions on external clippers.

    Add that to the clipping companies’ increased selectiveness and rising rates, and something’s gotta give, according to Brandy Merriweather, founder and senior PR executive at BSTarPR.

    “Many successful clipping pages have secured partnerships with gambling entities, music labels, creator management companies, creator collectives, and streaming platforms. Consequently, they are becoming more selective about which creators they post, their rates, and the frequency of posting for specific creators,” she said.

    Merriweather told Digiday she’s seen creators have to pay extra money to clippers to switch priority streaming platforms.

    “It’s a MASSIVE business filled with egos, narrative control, fabricated numbers, unethical and sometimes purposely false content all going to the highest bidder,” she stated. To avoid price gouging or unfair depictions, creators need to take clipping into their own hands. “What used to be a vehicle to gain visibility has now turned into an accountability stage that creators have no control over since many don’t own these pages. The creators, their families, and their teams are being used to create drama and fuel negativity which algorithms have prioritized because of the engagement….It’s a system many helped build that now controls them.”.

    Merriweather’s solution matches the other experts Digiday spoke with: creators have to create their own clipping networks to ensure they have control over their content and a proper understanding of how it’s performing.

    OpenAI revised its ChatGPT Business Hub terms following concerns that the original language could restrict businesses’ legal claims.

    Grand Theft Auto 6 has its own content creator cottage industry, with millions of views and a crowded, competitive marketplace.

    ChatGPT’s new AI visibility and click data can help inform publishers’ GEO strategies and complement third-party analytics.

    Industry News: Digiday+ Research: A-Frame Brands, Ritual and other brands prioritize newly introduced customer acquisition this holiday season

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that join us Dec.
    • This research is based on unique data collected from our proprietary audience of publisher, agency, brand and tech insiders.
    • As Black Friday and Cyber Monday rapidly approaches, brands are most focused on acquiring upcoming customers this holiday season.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    This research is based on unique data collected from our proprietary audience of publisher, agency, brand and tech insiders. It’s available to Digiday+ members. More from the series →.

    As Black Friday and Cyber Monday rapidly approaches, brands are most focused on acquiring upcoming customers this holiday season. They’re also eager to turn those seasonal shoppers into repeat buyers.

    Fifty-nine percent of brand and retailer professionals said that new customers are the primary audience for their 2026 holiday advertising. That’s down just one percentage point from the 60% of marketers who said the same last year, indicating that customer targeting trends have not shifted significantly.

    Less than half of survey respondents (41%) said that existing customers are the main audience for their holiday marketing, up one percentage point from 40% in 2025.

    The holiday season’s influx of shoppers gives brands an annual opportunity to attract fresh customers and to build lasting relationships beyond the initial purchase.

    Ari Bloom, founder and CEO of brand incubator A-Frame Brands, estimates that brands see a 20% to 30% increase in new customers as a percentage of total during the holiday season, as consumers look to discover products and brands. “It is a time period where you can acquire a lot of new customers… when we naturally see new customers come into the holiday funnel,” Bloom remarked.

    He also expects AI to play a central role in 2026 holiday marketing, changing how consumers find and buy products. “AI is probably going to become one of the most important funnels for upcoming customers because, instead of using old habits to discover existing brands, there’s a whole other ‘person’ shopping for them,” Bloom stated. “Just as we see people relying more on AI agents, you’re going to see more new brand exploration and customer acquisition from the brand side.”But acquiring new customers is only part of the equation. Brands also need to give existing customers a reason to return.

    Laura Brodie, chief growth officer at supplement company Ritual, noted brands can encourage repeat purchases by offering exclusive perks, seasonal products and other incentives. “Being able to pull people back who have shopped before by creating a compelling gift with purchase, seasonal drop or something similar is one way,” Brodie said. “If you don’t have the budget to support units, having something that feels intentional for an existing customer base is another.”.

    Brands with similar consumer bases should also consider partnering on gift-with-purchase offers, according to Brodie. “The cost of acquisition is high during the holidays, so being able to tap an existing audience can be really cost-effective,” she stated. “Similar-sized brands can create something that feels compelling [to consumers] and benefits both brands — potentially an offer swap. We’ve had success partnering with brands like Osea on a swap gift with purchases.”.

    As social trends accelerate, brands like General Mills are scoring creator posts for shareability to bridge the gap between organic buzz and paid media.

    Dick’s Sporting Goods is turning youth sports into a premium ad business

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, join us Dec.
    • Dick’s Sporting Goods has found that there’s big business in youth sports.
    • The sporting retailer recorded a third quarter GAAP net income of $161 million in earnings this week — more than double the $75 million reported the year prior.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    Dick’s Sporting Goods has found that there’s big business in youth sports.

    The sporting retailer recorded a third quarter GAAP net income of $161 million in earnings this week — more than double the $75 million reported the year prior.

    Dick’s execs attributed much of that success to Dick’s Media Network, home to its youth sports app GameChange.

    In a recent development, like many long-tail retail media networks, Dick’s Sporting Goods doesn’t break out its ad business revenue by dollar figure or percentage. Dick’s chief financial officer Navdeep Gupta noted that the organization is grappling with supply-chain related costs, higher fuel costs and other pressures, but Dick’s Media Network partially offset those pressures.

    “We have talked about these gross margin growth drivers with Dick’s Media Network and GameChanger. Those are continuing to be very differentiated drivers of not only our profitability, but our gross margin expansion,” he mentioned.

    Recent findings suggest that dick’s Media Network is four years old and offers ad units in-store, on its own site, off-site across the open web, social and streaming. Perhaps its biggest get is its live sports via GameChanger.

    “They found this gap in the marketplace in terms of sports club video streaming. And they’ve created this app, this solution, and now they inherently have their own O&O [owned and operated] inventory from a media perspective,” said Olivia Hawkins, vp of media strategy at Salt XC.

    Dick’s has previously worked with sports brands like Adidas, On, Under Armor and Crocs. However, the sports retailer is actively engaging non-endemic partners too.

    Industry observers note that take Chobani, for example. The yogurt brand bought ad space on Dick’s Sporting Goods Game Changer app during the 2026 FIFA World Cup, noted Hawkins, who was familiar with the deal.

    In a recent development, she did not disclose financial details of the ad buy. The campaign focused on reach and awareness, getting Chobani in front of youth sports enthusiasts, like parents and coaches, Hawkins said.

    “They met our expectations in terms of reaching a fresh audience and delivery, frequency, and all those media metrics — CPM and video completions and all that,” she said, without detailing the campaign’s success.

    Dick’s video app CPMs are more premium, hovering around $35, according to one commerce executive who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

    Sources indicate that “That’s more expensive than big TV. They’re asking for that price for that type of inventory. It’s a great solution — super clever, but it’s expensive,” the anonymous exec told Digiday. In comparison, Netflix CPMs fell from their initial $60 when it launched in 2022 to the low $20s presently.

    Seemingly, brands are willing to cough up the dough. That’s the bet Dick’s seems to be making. It makes sense given sports has become the industry’s latest golden goose.

    According to recent reports, put some numbers on it. In a survey this year, Dick’s Media and eMarketer reported that 63% of U.S. parents have kids in youth sports and 84% of them mentioned youth sports influence their buying choices.

    Now, there’s the question of scale. Dick’s GameChanger app has more than 5 million monthly active owners, but youth sports is more niche than something like the National Football League, which averages 18.7 million viewers per game during the regular season.

    “It’s a great audience. It’s a great inventory, but it is finite versus other offsite environments that include all of the open web,” Hawkins said.

    That leaves Dick’s in the same boat as other retail media networks — or at least every other RMN that isn’t Amazon or Walmart — where continued growth may have to come from beyond retailers’ owned and operated channels.

    Brands race to systematize how to know what makes creator content worth paying for

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (907 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Digiday

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that join us Dec.
    • It has been revealed that social media trends move faster than brands can keep up with.
    • Home to brands like Cheerios, Cinnamon Toast Crunch and Trix, the CPG brand has spent the past year putting together an internal framework to systematize monetizing viral moments.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit.

    It has been revealed that social media trends move faster than brands can keep up with. Now, they’re trying to create repeatable systems to turn organic social attention into something they can evaluate, fund and ultimately scale.

    Take General Mills, for example. Home to brands like Cheerios, Cinnamon Toast Crunch and Trix, the CPG brand has spent the past year putting together an internal framework to systematize monetizing viral moments.

    Sources indicate that its “talkability score” is a calculation used to measure whether General Mills’ brands are earning more attention with social media creators than they’re buying with paid ads. It’s a loose framework that varies by brand, Mindy Murray, director of influencer and content at General Mills said, and generates a score based on whether people shared it, put their own spin on it and how long interest in the trend lasts.

    It has been revealed that murray was mum on the actual mechanics on how it actually determines whether to invest ad spend. “We’re weighing on earning, we’re weighing things like active engagement — so shares likes, comments, saves — because we know that that means someone took an actual effort to do something versus just an impression,” Murray said.

    Virality can’t be manufactured, but this “operating system” allows them to “go faster and be smarter,” remarked Murray.

    Over the past year, General Mills has also reorganized its teams to bring social and influencer marketing under Murray’s purview, she told Digiday, to move more swiftly and efficiently in converting buzzy organic content into paid ads.

    For example, over the summer Reese’s “Eat ‘Em Up” cereal jingle from the early 2000s started trending on TikTok. General Mills noticed the trend, partnered with GloRilla to re-record the rap, tracked real-time activity via its framework, and ultimately turned it into a campaign on streaming platforms and Reese’s Puffs’ YouTube channel. The company boasted a 2.5% year-over-year sales increase as a result, but did not provide specific sales figures. The company did not say specifically how the framework informed that strategy.

    Last week, influencer agency Billion Dollar Boy (BDB) rolled out its Creator Investment Planner, a financial modeling tool that aims to help marketers understand the ad spend levels required to initiative and “de-risk creator investments,” according to a news release.

    BDB’s tool works by calculating blended CPMs from creators and social media platforms. Marketers enter their budget and time frame, and the platform calculates estimates for share of voice, total impressions and earned media value. Per BDB, the model can update as inputs change, where marketers can expect to “de-risk” spend commitments.

    And in April, CreatorIQ creator platform and creative analytics and governance platform CreativeX released a newly introduced tool to help brands incorporate creator content into a paid media strategy. The system works on an API, sending creator content from CreatorIQ’s platform to CreativeX to be graded, reviewed by CreativeX’s AI-powered system and optimized by a brand campaign manager. Ultimately, it aims to identify creator posts with potential to do well as an ad before any media buyers open their wallets. Nestlé was the first brand to sign on. The integration was announced on an invite-only basis.

    To agency execs, all signs point to brands getting more rigorous about their spend — especially when it comes to squeezing performance out of creators — and do it before the trend disappears.

    Industry observers note that creator spend is expected to increase 12% every year until 2030, according to advertising research firm Madison & Wall. In no small part, brand spend on boosting or promoting creator content is fueling that growth.

    “Before any sort of budget is unlocked, you have to be able to prove out that there’s a higher propensity for that piece of content for whatever investment you’re making into social to actually move towards a conversion,” stated Madison Gaudry-Routledge, evp of social at Viral Nation, a social agency.

    Most brands, Gaudry-Routledge mentioned, haven’t come up with a named framework in the same way General Mills has. Brand spend on creator marketing is expected to grow twice as fast as spending on advertising. Naturally, brands are eager to see proof of concept as early as possible.

    Industry observers note that viral Nation has its own proprietary framework offered to clients as an add-on service. It’s called Culture Quotient that blends brand awareness, brand affinity and brand velocity into a measurable score to determine a brand’s relevance in cultural conversation. The tool works via AI that analyzes conversations and content, identifies emerging cultural trends and tracks shifts in consumer sentiment, per Gaudry-Routledge. The social exec declined to share any client-specific examples.

    These calculations are being built in real time and haven’t yet replaced traditional metrics like share of voice, audience sentiment and engagement.

    “As an industry, we’re continuing to try to catch up on operationalizing frameworks and systematizing measurement and still not there yet,” remarked Kristina Coughlin, svp and general manager of Trevant, a creator marketing agency.

    Is it really even Thanksgiving if a giant, monocled peanut in a top hat doesn’t strut down the streets of Manhattan? This year, for Planters, the answer is no.

    The snacking brand is bringing Mr. Peanut back to Macy’s annual Thanksgiving Day Parade for the first time in a decade, and it’s not the only brand set to make a splash or debut as the tradition marks its 100th year.

    With last year’s event the most-watched American entertainment program of the year, drawing a record 35.7 million viewers, brands like Levi’s, DoorDash, and Geico are now joining the celebrations for the first time, along with around 100 other balloons.

    Learn our default setups, decision log and the core and vendor systems around your product.

    Our company is growing swiftly, and so is our team. We're looking for people who want to help shape a world-class delivery motion.

    Experience with self-managed or on-premises software where vendor visibility is limited.

    Hands-on experience running AI or automation programs, including using tools like Claude to build analyses, prototypes or agent workflows.

    Nice to have: familiarity with process orchestration or Camunda's customer base.
